findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Give AC3 a concrete proving method: decode the rendered base64gzip payload and byte-diff it against the prior rendered user_data.sh (deterministic, in-session), AND state how cloud-init acceptance of the gzip encoding is validated (e.g. a throwaway instance / cloud-init boot drill) or record explicit rationale for deferring the boot check.
evidence: AC3: 'The rendered user-data still works: cloud-init accepts the encoding and the script's behaviour on boot is unchanged.'
AC2 requires 'aws_instance.gerrit is NOT replaced' — so user_data change only takes effect on next boot, per the plan's own note that it 'only takes effect on next boot'
No decode-and-diff or boot-drill step is described to prove AC3
findings.finding: AC3 asserts the rendered user-data 'still works' and 'behaviour on boot is unchanged' but names no proving command, and the gzip-encoding cutover path is not exercised end-to-end; combined with AC2 (instance NOT replaced), the new base64gzip user_data will not execute until a next boot, so on-boot behaviour cannot be observed in-session.
scenarios: base64gzip renders but cloud-init on the target AMI/version rejects or mishandles the gzip magic, silently breaking the next reboot
the decoded payload differs from the pre-change rendered script and nobody notices because no comparison is run
findings.suggested_fix: Add: 'AC3a: `terraform console`/templatefile render piped through `base64 -d | gunzip` byte-matches the current rendered script (diff empty). AC3b: gzip user-data accepted by cloud-init proven on a disposable instance, or deferred with rationale since aws_instance.gerrit is not rebooted by this change.'

findings.checklist_item: State how AC3 exercises the gzipped payload end-to-end — e.g. boot a throwaway EC2 instance with the new user_data_base64 and confirm cloud-init decodes and runs it, or run a local cloud-init render/decode validation — rather than asserting 'behaviour on boot is unchanged'.
evidence: AC3: 'The rendered user-data still works: cloud-init accepts the encoding and the script's behaviour on boot is unchanged.'
Hazard note: 'an in-place attribute update that only takes effect on next boot'
AC2 requires aws_instance.gerrit NOT replaced, so the live host does not re-run user_data during this change
findings.finding: AC3 requires 'the script's behaviour on boot is unchanged' but the plan's own hazard note establishes user_data changes only take effect on next boot, and AC2 requires the running instance NOT be replaced — so the new gzipped payload is never actually executed by the live host during this change. AC3 does not state HOW the encoded payload's boot behaviour is exercised (a scratch/test instance boot, a `cloud-init` local schema/render validation, or a decode round-trip check). A broken encoding would pass green and only surface at a future replacement/boot.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an explicit verification step: base64gzip round-trip decode equals the templatefile output, AND a disposable instance (or `cloud-init devel schema` / local render) confirms cloud-init accepts the gzip encoding and completes the script, before closing AC3.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State AC4's default in the plan: the guard measures the RENDERED/base64gzip-encoded payload against 16,384 bytes (the value AWS actually receives), not the raw source file.
evidence: AC4: 'State whether the guard measures the RAW file or the RENDERED/encoded payload, and justify which is correct.'
Plan's remedy is 'user_data_base64 = base64gzip(templatefile(...))' — after this fix the raw file stays ~16,666 bytes but the encoded payload is far smaller
findings.finding: AC4 defers the RAW-vs-RENDERED guard-measurement decision to the executor ('State whether the guard measures the RAW file or the RENDERED/encoded payload, and justify which is correct') without stating the default, even though the plan's own facts settle it: the 16,384-byte AWS limit applies to the user_data attribute AWS receives, i.e. the base64gzip-encoded payload, not the raw source file.
scenarios: executor guards the RAW 16,666-byte file and the CI check false-fails immediately after the gzip fix (raw still over 16384)
executor guards the raw file and the guard never reflects the real AWS limit on the encoded payload
findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite AC4 to fix the decision: 'The guard measures the rendered base64gzip-encoded user_data (the payload AWS enforces the 16,384-byte limit on), not the raw source file, and fails at commit/CI time when that encoded size exceeds the limit.'

findings.checklist_item: Note that terraform-drift.yml's `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` already returns 1=error vs 2=drift, and specify AC5 as surfacing/labelling the existing exit-1 (plan-failed) path distinctly rather than building a new detection mechanism.

AC5: 'The distinction between "plan failed to generate" and "drift detected" is visible in the drift workflow's output'
findings.finding: AC5 mandates making the 'plan failed to generate' vs 'drift detected' distinction visible in the drift workflow, but terraform-drift.yml already runs `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode`, whose exit codes ALREADY separate these conditions (0=no changes, 2=drift, 1=error). The plan does not acknowledge this existing tool-level signal, risking a net-new distinction mechanism that reinvents what the exit code already provides — the gap is surfacing/labelling exit-1 distinctly, not building new detection.
scenarios: Author adds a separate parsing/classification mechanism instead of branching on the existing -detailed-exitcode value (1 vs 2) already emitted by the plan step

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the measured gzipped size and resulting base64-encoded length of the rendered user-data (confirming it clears 16,384 with the base64 ~33% overhead accounted for), so the 'years of headroom' claim is quantified and AC4's guard has a concrete budget.
evidence: Plan: 'at 73% comments this file compresses very well, so it buys years of headroom'
Mechanism fact: user_data_base64 is validated as a base64 string, which is ~4/3 the size of the gzip binary; the plan gives no number for either
AC1 only asserts 'terraform plan GENERATES successfully' — it empirically catches a miss but the plan states no expected sizing
findings.finding: The plan claims base64gzip 'buys years of headroom' but never states a measured or estimated size of the compressed+base64-encoded payload. With user_data_base64 the AWS provider validates the BASE64 STRING length (~33% larger than the raw gzip bytes), so the gzipped script must be under ~12,288 bytes for the base64 form to clear 16,384. The headroom claim rests on an unverified compression ratio.
scenarios: Future edits re-add enough content that the gzipped+base64 payload creeps back toward 16,384 without warning, since no target headroom figure was ever recorded
